name: Salicylic acid peel

lead: A salicylic acid peel is the superficial peel most often used for acne and some pigmentation. People use it for clearer pores, fewer breakouts and fewer marks.

Salicylic acid is a beta-hydroxy acid described as antibacterial, anti-inflammatory and oil-soluble, which is why it is associated with acne-prone skin. Studies commonly use 20 to 30% concentrations. Published work is mostly small comparative studies and registered trials, such as a 2014 study comparing pyruvic and salicylic peels on sebum secretion in 20 people with acne.

paras: A clinician applies it in the office, and it is often repeated as a series of sessions spaced weeks apart. Mild flaking is typical, and people usually keep up sunscreen and acne skincare alongside it.
Light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness. Deeper peels carry higher complication risks such as pigment change.

angle.text: People use salicylic acid peels to clear acne and reduce the marks it leaves. The oil-soluble acid works into pores, easing breakouts and inflammation so skin looks clearer. Small comparative studies cover its acne use.

lead: A salicylic acid peel is a superficial chemical peel using salicylic acid, a beta-hydroxy acid (BHA), commonly at 20 to 30% in clinical studies and used mainly for acne and pigmentation [1][2]. Wikipedia describes salicylic acid as antibacterial and anti-inflammatory and increasingly preferred over AHAs because it is oil-soluble, though the oil-solubility claim is flagged there as needing a citation [3].
Published evidence consists mostly of small comparative studies and registered trials. A 2014 study compared 50% pyruvic and 30% salicylic peels on sebum secretion in 20 people with acne [1].

paras: The 2014 comparison of 50% pyruvic acid and 30% salicylic acid peels in 20 men and women aged 13 to 30 with acne measured facial sebum secretion [1].

Registered trials have compared 30% salicylic acid with 25% trichloroacetic acid in mild to moderate acne (60 participants, completed) [2], combined it with 4% hydroquinone for melasma in Hispanic women [4], compared it with glycolic acid for melasma [5] and for post-acne scars [6], and compared peel types in acne [7]. Results of these registrations are not summarized in the available records.

Wikipedia notes that complications rise with peel depth and can include prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia and skin thinning, and that light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness. [3]
